vo2-plateau.short: In a test where the work keeps rising, the point near the top where oxygen uptake stops rising (or rises far less than the extra work needs). The classic sign that VO₂max has been reached.

incremental-test.short: A test in which power or speed rises in steps (every minute or few) or smoothly (a ramp) until you can't go on. The standard way to measure VO₂max.

secondary-criteria.short: Cut-offs used to accept a test as maximal when no VO₂ plateau shows: for example a high RER, a heart rate near the predicted maximum, or a high blood lactate.

verification-bout.short: A second effort to exhaustion at a constant power (about 110% of the ramp test's top power), after a short rest. If VO₂ goes no higher than in the ramp, the ramp's peak was the true VO₂max.

central-limit.short: The view that VO₂max is set by oxygen delivery: mainly how much blood the heart can pump per minute and how much O₂ each litre of blood carries.

peripheral-limit.short: The view that VO₂max is set in the working muscle: how well it can take O₂ out of the blood and use it (its capillaries and mitochondria).

blood-doping.short: Raising the number of red cells to carry more O₂: by putting stored blood back in (a transfusion) or with drugs such as EPO. Banned in sport.

hyperoxia.short: Breathing air with more oxygen in it than normal air's 21%, in the lab from a gas tank or bag.

fractional-utilisation.short: The share of your VO₂max you can keep up for a given race or duration, such as 85%. Set mostly by your lactate thresholds.

performance-vo2.short: The oxygen uptake you can keep up for a whole race: VO₂max × fractional utilisation (Joyner and Coyle's term).

range-restriction.short: When everyone in a study has similar values of a measure (say, all elites with a high VO₂max), that measure shows little link with the outcome, even if it matters a lot across all people.

hiit.short: Training in repeated hard bouts, from seconds to a few minutes, near or above the intensity that draws out VO₂max, with easier recovery between them.

continuous-training.short: Training at a steady, mostly moderate intensity without breaks, such as a 1-hour ride or run at an even pace.

fat-free-mass.short: Everything in the body that isn't fat: muscle, bone, organs and water. Lean mass is almost the same thing (it leaves out bone mineral).

masters-athlete.short: An athlete competing in age-group categories, usually from about 35 or 40 years old, often still training hard.
